tip: German has no -ing tense. 'Gerade' marks something happening right now: 'lernt gerade die fünfte'.
'Weil' sends the verb to the end of its clause: 'weil der letzte Bus schon abgefahren ist', with 'ist' last.
The particle 'doch' reminds the listener of something known: 'du hast doch gesagt' = you did say.
With no article, the adjective itself carries the case ending: 'mit frischem Brot', where '-em' marks the dative 'dem' would have shown.
'Möchte' (would like) is polite. 'Ich will einen Kaffee' sounds blunt (literally 'I want'). Say 'ich möchte einen Kaffee' instead.
German yes/no questions need no 'do': 'Hast du Geschwister' is literally 'Have you siblings', verb first.
Regular verbs add '-st' in the 'du' form: 'lernen' becomes 'du lernst'.
Verbs of motion normally build the perfect with 'sein', not 'haben': 'wir sind angekommen'.
'Na' is a casual opener, like 'so' or 'well': 'Na, wie ist die Lage?'
'Vergessen' switches 'e' to 'i' in the 'du' and 'er' forms: 'du vergisst'.
After 'sind' the profession has no article: 'sie sind Lehrer'; even singular 'er ist Lehrer' = he is a teacher.
The possessive ending agrees with the owned noun: 'Farbe' is feminine, so it takes '-e' in 'seine Farbe'.
Future tense: 'werden' plus an infinitive at the end, 'du wirst ... finden'.
After 'den', the adjective ends in '-en': 'den schneebedeckten Gipfel'.
Separable verb 'ausgraben' splits: the prefix 'aus' jumps to the end, 'gräbt ... aus'.
After another verb, 'hören' stays an infinitive in the perfect: 'hat ... spielen hören', not 'gehört'.
'Es freut mich' is literally 'it pleases me'; the person is the object 'mich'.
Add 'gern' to a verb to say you enjoy doing it: 'sie tanzt gern' = likes to dance.
Lowercase day plus '-s' means 'every': 'montags' = on Mondays, as a routine.
'Studieren' is for university study; use 'lernen' for school learning: 'er studiert Jura'.
A definite time point takes the accusative: 'nächsten Monat', not 'nächster'.
'In' for a static location takes the dative: 'in einem Büro' answers 'where'.
After 'das', the adjective ends in '-e': 'das glühende Eisen'.
'Durch' always takes the accusative, so 'der Sturm' becomes 'durch den Sturm'.
With a time word, German uses the present for the future: 'ich habe morgen ...' = will have.
'Zur' is short for 'zu der', the dative: 'zur Arbeit' means 'to work'.
'Glück haben' means 'to be lucky', literally 'to have luck': 'wir haben Glück gehabt'.
'Zeigen' takes a dative person for the receiver: 'sie zeigt mir' = shows to me.
'Werden' also means 'to get' or 'become': 'das Wetter wird besser' = will get better.
'Ins' is 'in' plus 'das'; motion into takes the accusative: 'ins Bett gehen'.
